Simple Linear Regression Slope

Source: R/slr_slope.R
slr_slope.Rd

Calculates the ordinary least squares slope of the simple linear regression of y on x: the expected change in y for a one unit increase in x. This is the point estimate used by the sequential procedure seq_aipe_reg_coef.

Usage

slr_slope(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector, the predictor.

y

A numeric vector, the outcome. It must have the same length as x; the two are paired by position.

na.rm

Should a pair be removed when either of its values is missing? Default TRUE. With na.rm = FALSE a missing value is an error.

Value

A single number, the estimated slope, in units of y per unit of x. At least two complete pairs are needed, and x must vary: a predictor with no variation is an error, because the slope is then undefined. Values of x that agree to ten significant digits count as no variation (such differences are usually rounding error); if they are real, subtract a constant from x first. A slope too large for a double (which takes units of y and x more than about 300 orders of magnitude apart) is an error that says so.

Details

The slope is \(b_1 = s_{xy} / s_x^2\), the sample covariance of x and y divided by the sample variance of x (Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay, 2018, Equation 35). It is the same number as coef(lm(y ~ x))[2].

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

See also

seq_aipe_reg_coef; in DMAR, ci_reg_coef for a fixed sample size confidence interval.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Hours of training and a performance rating for eight employees.
hours  <- c(2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15)
rating <- c(48, 55, 53, 61, 66, 64, 73, 80)
slr_slope(hours, rating)
#> [1] 2.403056
